findings.text: Within the first three short paragraphs, a newcomer learns what Athena is, what a study is, and that this page is a study of another project. That answers 'what is this' quickly.
findings.source: <header> lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: Athena's home URL opens on a detailed study of a different project, firstmate. Athena itself gets one sentence. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena may wonder which project the page is about, and gets very little on why Athena matters to them.
What to do next is easy to find. A link near the top jumps to the steps, and the steps give the repository link, an install command, and a sample request.
findings.source: header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the "Next steps" section

findings.text: The install steps leave gaps. There is no clone command, no list of what you need first (for example model access or API keys), and no description of what `athena ask` produces. A newcomer probably has to visit the repository before they can try it.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" / "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: 'Start here' opens with seven internal firstmate terms before the reader knows why they matter. 'in scope' is admitted to be undefined. This is heavy going for someone who just wants the overview.
findings.source: Start here > Words used first: "yolo", "in scope", "green", "red", "local-only landing"

findings.text: Ids are used before they are explained: transitions are cited before the Transitions section, and 'ra' ids are never explained. Together with the bracketed claim ids on every line, this makes the body read like a spec, not an introduction.
findings.source: Counters: "changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"; Why it is built this way: "ra1" … "ra6"

findings.text: Some sections are about how the page was produced, not about either project. They are honest about the study's limits, but they add bulk a newcomer does not need and could confuse them.
findings.source: Limits of this study f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths…"; About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/"

findings.text: Every claim links to exact lines at a pinned commit, so a careful reader can check the traceability the page promises for themselves. This is the clearest evidence of why Athena matters, but the page never spells out that benefit for the reader.
findings.source: Next steps: "Check a statement: follow a bracketed claim id to the claim, then its source link to the file and lines in firstmate at the pinned commit."
